**Title**
Why Token Pruning Crashes Some Robot Policies but Not Others: Vision Connectors and VLA Token Compressibility

**Abstract**
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models consume hundreds of vision tokens per frame, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time robotic control. Token pruning offers a training-free remedy, yet whether a pruning strategy transfers across architectures is untested: the same 5% removal collapses one VLA to near-zero success while another retains full performance.
We conduct a systematic study of token compressibility across six VLA architectures (450M–7B parameters), three vision-connector families, and four LIBERO manipulation suites.
Two axes govern the pruning response and interact to produce a *double dissociation*.
Along the **coupling axis**, token-independent connectors (linear projections, MLPs) degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors (pixel-shuffle, learned encoders) exhibit threshold cliffs or complete collapse.
Along the **complexity axis**, multi-step tasks amplify entangling-connector losses by up to 20× relative to single-step tasks, whereas independent connectors show ≤11 pp amplification under the same conditions.
The two axes cross in scoring-method effectiveness: attention-based selection recovers +31 pp on an entangling connector but degrades performance (−2 to −30 pp) on an independent one; norm-based selection shows the converse.
No single pruning recipe is universally safe: even on one architecture, L2 norm outperforms random by +8 pp on one suite yet underperforms by −5 pp on another.
The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms, computable in one forward pass, predicts both the compressibility class and the scoring-method sign, providing a practical diagnostic without closed-loop evaluation.
For architectures where every deletion strategy fails, a lightweight re-encoding module (~5% extra parameters) recovers >60% success rate at 75% compression, establishing deletion itself—not token redundancy—as the failure mechanism.

**Primary Keyword**
Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems

\begin{abstract}
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models consume hundreds of vision tokens per frame, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time robotic control. Token pruning offers a training-free remedy, yet whether a pruning strategy transfers across architectures remains untested: the same mild removal collapses one VLA to near-zero success while another retains full performance.
We conduct a systematic study of token compressibility across six VLA architectures spanning 450M to 7B parameters, three vision-connector families, and four LIBERO manipulation suites.
Two axes govern the pruning response and interact to produce a \emph{double dissociation}.
Along the \textbf{coupling axis}, token-independent connectors (linear projections, MLPs) degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors (pixel-shuffle, learned encoders) exhibit threshold cliffs or complete collapse.
Along the \textbf{complexity axis}, multi-step tasks disproportionately amplify entangling-connector losses, whereas independent connectors remain comparatively stable under the same conditions.
The two axes cross in scoring-method effectiveness: attention-based selection substantially recovers performance on entangling connectors but degrades it on independent ones; norm-based selection shows the converse.
No single pruning recipe is universally safe---even within one architecture, the best scoring method reverses between task suites.
The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms, computable in a single forward pass, predicts both the compressibility class and the scoring-method sign, providing a practical diagnostic without closed-loop evaluation.
For architectures where every deletion strategy fails, a lightweight re-encoding module recovers strong performance at high compression, establishing deletion itself---not token redundancy---as the failure mechanism.
\end{abstract}
